1	# AI assistants (MCP setup)
2	
3	DataQ ships a built-in [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server so AI assistants — Claude Desktop, Claude.ai, VS Code / GitHub Copilot, Cursor — can answer questions like *"what failed today?"* or *"run the orders suite"* against your live DataQ instance, with the same per-suite permissions as the signed-in user.
4	
5	## Endpoint & authentication
6	
7	The server is mounted on the deployed app at:
8	
9	```text
10	https://<your-dataq-host>/mcp/
11	```
12	
13	!!! warning "Keep the trailing slash"
14	    `/mcp` answers with a **307 redirect** to `/mcp/`, and some HTTP clients drop the
15	    `Authorization` header when following redirects — which then surfaces as a
16	    confusing 401. Always configure clients with the `/mcp/` form.
17	
18	The endpoint accepts the **same credentials as the REST API** (ADR [0008](adr/0008-mcp-server.md) / [0026](adr/0026-auth-api-keys-and-principal-seam.md)): an OIDC bearer token (Azure AD or Cognito), or a **DataQ API key** (`dq_live_…`). Without auth configured, the endpoint is only mounted in local dev-bypass mode — never unauthenticated in a deployed environment.
19	
20	!!! info "Email-OTP deployments: MCP works, with an API key"
21	    A deployment running **email one-time codes instead of SSO** (ADR
22	    [0032](adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md)) has no identity provider to issue bearer
23	    tokens, so an **API key is the only `/mcp` credential** there — mint one as
24	    below and use it exactly the same way. Everything else is identical, including
25	    all 46 tools and per-suite permissions. Two rejections are deliberate in that
26	    mode: a raw JWT is refused (there is nothing to validate it against), and your
27	    **sign-in session is never accepted** — it is a browser credential and does not
28	    authenticate `/mcp`, whether presented as a bearer or carried as a cookie.
29	
30	### Getting a token
31	
32	**Recommended — a DataQ API key (PAT):** mint one via `POST /api/v1/me/api-keys`
33	(see [API keys](api-keys.md)) and use it as the bearer. It lives up to a year,
34	is revocable per-integration, and runs with exactly your per-suite access —
35	built for always-on MCP configs.
36	
37	**Quick one-off — your web session's OIDC token:** sign in to the DataQ web
38	app, open your browser's developer tools → **Application → Session Storage** →
39	the `oidc.user:…` entry → copy the `access_token` value.
40	
41	!!! note "OIDC tokens expire after ~1 hour"
42	    The pasted browser token is short-lived; when the client starts getting
43	    401s, paste a fresh one and restart the MCP server/connection — or switch
44	    to an [API key](api-keys.md) and stop re-pasting.
45	
46	!!! danger "Never commit a config that carries a token"
47	    Keep token-bearing MCP config files out of version control (in the DataQ repo
48	    itself, `.gitignore` already covers `.vscode/*`).
49	
50	## Client configuration
51	
52	**Claude Desktop / Claude.ai** (`claude_desktop_config.json`) — and **GitHub Copilot** (`mcp.json`):
53	
54	```jsonc
55	{
56	  "mcpServers": {
57	    "dataq": {
58	      "url": "https://<your-dataq-host>/mcp/",
59	      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <AZURE_AD_ACCESS_TOKEN>" }
60	    }
61	  }
62	}
63	```
64	
65	**VS Code** (workspace `.vscode/mcp.json`, used by Copilot agent mode) uses a `servers` key — not `mcpServers` — plus an explicit `type`:
66	
67	```jsonc
68	{
69	  "servers": {
70	    "dataq": {
71	      "type": "http",
72	      "url": "https://<your-dataq-host>/mcp/",
73	      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <AZURE_AD_ACCESS_TOKEN>" }
74	    }
75	  }
76	}
77	```
78	
79	Start it via the command palette (`Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P`) → **MCP: List Servers** → *dataq* → Start (or open Copilot Chat in agent mode — configured servers start on demand).
80	
81	**Cursor** (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`) uses the same `mcpServers` shape as Claude Desktop.
82	
83	## The 46 tools
84	
85	Each tool is a thin wrapper over the same service layer as the REST API — per-suite
86	authorization (`view` for a read, `edit` for a mutation) and failing-sample redaction apply
87	identically. The 46 split three ways, not two:
88	
89	- **23 read-only** — `export_suite`, `get_adf_pipeline_status`, `get_asset`, `get_check`,
90	  `get_check_history`, `get_column_policy`, `get_health_score`, `get_incident`,
91	  `get_near_misses`, `get_notification_config`, `get_run_results`, `get_run_status`,
92	  `get_suite_performance`, `get_suite_results`, `list_assets`, `list_check_versions`,
93	  `list_checks`, `list_connections`, `list_incidents`, `list_runs`, `list_schedules`,
94	  `list_suites`, `list_trigger_bindings`.
95	- **18 that change state** — `create_check`, `update_check`, `delete_check`, `snooze_check`,
96	  `restore_check_version`, `trigger_suite_run`, `cancel_run`, `update_suite`, `set_column_policy`,
97	  `create_schedule`, `update_schedule`, `delete_schedule`, `create_trigger_binding`,
98	  `update_trigger_binding`, `delete_trigger_binding`, `ack_incident`, `resolve_incident`,
99	  `import_suite`. All gate on `edit` access to the affected suite (the schedule, binding and
100	  incident tools via the suite they target); `import_suite` additionally requires the **member**
101	  workspace role, since it has no existing suite to gate on.
102	- **5 that persist nothing but open a live datasource connection using stored credentials** —
103	  `profile_column`, `list_columns`, `dryrun_check`, `suggest_column_policy`, `test_connection`.
104	  These are gated like writes, not like reads, because they spend a real credential against a
105	  remote system even though nothing is saved: the first four require `edit` on the suite whose
106	  connection they probe, and `test_connection` (which has no suite at all) requires the **member**
107	  workspace role.
108	
109	No MCP tool is Admin-only. Every Admin-only capability in ADR 0033's authorization matrix is a
110	connection *mutation* (create/edit/delete/re-auth), and none of those are exposed here at all —
111	a credential must never transit an LLM. `test_connection` reports only whether a live probe
112	succeeded; it never returns a credential or a secret reference (Tier 1 + Tier 2 expansion, issue
113	[#529](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/529)).
114	
115	### Reading the results honestly
116	
117	A REST caller wrote their own query and a UI user reads the screen — the row
118	count, the timestamps, the "running" badge, the filter they chose. An AI client
119	has neither, so several tools return **fields whose whole job is to say what the
120	answer does not cover**. A well-behaved client should branch on these rather
121	than summarising the payload as-is.
122	
123	| Field | Appears on | What it prevents |
124	|---|---|---|
125	| `total` · `returned` · `truncated` | `list_runs`, `list_checks`, `list_check_versions`, `list_incidents`, `list_assets`, `get_check_history`, `get_adf_pipeline_status` | reporting one page as the whole set. `truncated` is computed against a real total, never inferred from page length. The unpaged tools — `list_suites`, `list_connections`, `list_schedules`, `list_trigger_bindings`, `get_near_misses` — return every row and carry no page fields at all |
126	| `oldest_in_page` · `newest_in_page` | `list_runs`, `get_check_history`, `get_adf_pipeline_status` | answering a time-bounded question ("what failed today?") from a **count**-capped page. None of these tools has a time filter ([#1442](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1442)) — these fields say what window you actually saw |
127	| `results_final` | `list_runs`, `get_run_results`, `get_run_status`, `get_suite_results` | reading a mid-run partial as a verdict. A 30-check suite three checks in genuinely has "3/3 passed" — and no result yet |
128	| `redaction` · `redacted_columns` | per-check results | describing masked rows as "no failing rows", or mask tokens as data |
129	| `sampling` · `sampled` · `sample_row_limit` | results, `profile_column` | stating a sample statistic as a fact about the full dataset |
130	| `runnable` | `update_suite`, `import_suite` | reporting a suite as ready when it has no run target and cannot run |

# Changelog

Notable, user-facing changes. Dates are the release/merge date. This is a curated summary —
the per-PR history lives in the repo's commit log and pull requests.

## Unreleased

### Changed

- **MCP `list_runs`/`list_incidents` gained `since_hours`/`until_hours` time
  filters** (#1442): both were count-capped only, so "what failed today" was
  answered with "the 20 most recent runs" — correct on a quiet workspace,
  wrong on a busy one. The offsets are relative to now ("N hours ago"), not
  clock times, so a caller doesn't need to know the server's current time.
  `list_incidents` also now states its auto-resolve blind spot (#1445): an
  incident auto-resolves on the first passing result, so a failure that has
  since recovered won't appear under `status="open"` even inside a matching
  time window — `list_runs`/`get_check_history` answer "what failed during
  period X", `list_incidents` answers "what's unresolved now". Its pagination
  now sorts by `last_seen_at` (the filter field) instead of `created_at`, so a
  truncated page is a contiguous slice of the window being asked about.

- **Unity Catalog checks now execute on the Databricks SQL Warehouse by default**
  (#1532): the built-in catalog expectations join custom SQL on one GX
  Databricks-SQL batch, so the warehouse evaluates them and worker memory stays

def test_list_orders_by_most_recent_breach_not_when_first_opened(
    client: TestClient, world: dict[str, Any]
) -> None:
    """#1442: `list_incidents` (shared by REST and MCP) sorts by `last_seen_at`,
    not `created_at` — an incident opened earlier that breached again most
    recently must lead the list, since "is this still happening" is about
    recent activity, not when the pair first paired up.
    """
    db = client_db(client)
    older = world["incident"]  # opened first, in the `world` fixture
    newer = _incident(db, world["suite"])  # opened second, on a different check
    assert older.created_at < newer.created_at

    # Re-breach the OLDER incident's check — attaches an occurrence and bumps
    # its last_seen_at ahead of the newer incident's.
    run = Run(
        suite_id=world["suite"].id,
        status="succeeded",
        triggered_by="t",
        asset_id=world["suite"].asset_id,
    )
    db.add(run)
    db.flush()
    db.add(Result(run_id=run.id, check_id=older.check_id, status="fail", metric_value=0.5))
    db.commit()
    incident_service.sync_incidents_for_run(db, run_id=run.id)

    _as(world["owner"])
    ids = [i["id"] for i in client.get("/api/v1/incidents").json()]
    assert ids.index(str(older.id)) < ids.index(str(newer.id))

def test_list_orders_by_most_recent_breach_not_when_first_opened(
    client: TestClient, world: dict[str, Any]
) -> None:
    """#1442: `list_incidents` (shared by REST and MCP) sorts by `last_seen_at`,
    not `created_at` — an incident opened earlier that breached again most
    recently must lead the list, since "is this still happening" is about
    recent activity, not when the pair first paired up.
    """
    db = client_db(client)
    older = world["incident"]  # opened first, in the `world` fixture
    newer = _incident(db, world["suite"])  # opened second, on a different check
    # `func.now()` is transaction-time in Postgres, so both timestamps tie
    # within one test transaction — force the ordering explicitly rather than
    # relying on wall-clock drift between the two `_incident()` calls.
    now = datetime.now(UTC)
    older.created_at = now - timedelta(hours=2)
    older.last_seen_at = now - timedelta(hours=2)
    newer.created_at = now - timedelta(hours=1)
    newer.last_seen_at = now - timedelta(hours=1)
    db.commit()

    # Re-breach the OLDER incident's check — attaches an occurrence and bumps
    # its last_seen_at ahead of the newer incident's.
    run = Run(
        suite_id=world["suite"].id,
        status="succeeded",
        triggered_by="t",
        asset_id=world["suite"].asset_id,
    )
    db.add(run)
    db.flush()
    db.add(Result(run_id=run.id, check_id=older.check_id, status="fail", metric_value=0.5))
    db.commit()
    incident_service.sync_incidents_for_run(db, run_id=run.id)

    _as(world["owner"])
    ids = [i["id"] for i in client.get("/api/v1/incidents").json()]
    assert ids.index(str(older.id)) < ids.index(str(newer.id))

1	# Changelog
2	
3	Notable, user-facing changes. Dates are the release/merge date. This is a curated summary —
4	the per-PR history lives in the repo's commit log and pull requests.
5	
6	## Unreleased
7	
8	### Changed
9	
10	- **Unity Catalog checks now execute on the Databricks SQL Warehouse by default**
11	  (#1532): the built-in catalog expectations join custom SQL on one GX
12	  Databricks-SQL batch, so the warehouse evaluates them and worker memory stays
13	  flat regardless of table size (the Snowflake execution shape). Suites with a
14	  declared sample, `expect_column_values_to_be_of_type`, and unrecognised types
15	  stay on the previous read-into-pandas path; `UC_SQL_PUSHDOWN=false` restores
16	  the old routing wholesale. ⚠ Checks evaluated by the warehouse follow *its*
17	  semantics — most visibly `expect_column_values_to_match_regex`, which now uses
18	  Spark/Java regex instead of Python `re` on Unity Catalog; a pattern relying on
19	  Python-only constructs may report differently. Flip the flag if a check's
20	  behavior looks changed and file what you find.
21	
22	## v1.1.0 — 2026-08-21
23	
24	Portability, auto-monitors, compliance-grade controls, and polish on top of v1. (First
25	tagged 2026-08-15; the tag was moved to the true cycle close on 2026-08-21 after the
26	stretch week landed the RBAC, MCP-expansion, security-audit and compliance tracks below.)
27	
28	- **Append-only audit trail (ADR 0041)** — every config mutation (35 routes: checks,
29	  connections, shares, roles, schedules, credential rotations, …) writes an `audit_events`
30	  row **inside the mutation's transaction**, with actor, before/after, and `request_id`;
31	  **data reads are audited too**: reading a run's results, downloading a comparison
32	  report, profiling a column or dry-running a check records who accessed which data and
33	  **whether regulated data was actually surfaced**. Workspace-admin read endpoint
34	  (`GET /api/v1/admin/audit-events`), own retention clock. Verified in production on both
35	  clouds.
36	- **Warehouse-tag PII classification** — DataQ reads the column classifications a
37	  customer already applied in their own warehouse (Snowflake `dataq_classification` +
38	  `PRIVACY_CATEGORY`, Unity Catalog `dataq_classification`) and feeds them into the
39	  redaction ladder as a floor a suite policy cannot lift — on REST, MCP and alert
40	  delivery. Plus an opt-in **fail-closed mode** (`require_classification`): nothing
41	  row-level surfaces unless a column is explicitly cleared. Live-verified on both
42	  warehouses.
43	- **Redaction follows the destination** — an author's own interactive preview keeps its
44	  values (and is audited); the same data headed to an LLM context, a file export or an
45	  alert is redacted. Scalar `observed_value`s (a MAX/MIN is a real cell) now mask under
46	  the same rules as lists, resolved against the check's **historical** config so editing
47	  a check can never retroactively relabel old results.
48	- **Residency & encryption posture** — a declared `DEPLOYMENT_REGION` surfaced at
49	  `GET /api/v1/admin/deployment`, an IaC postcondition that fails the plan if the compute
50	  environment leaves the declared region, and a per-resource encryption-at-rest table for
51	  both reference deployments in the security docs.
52	- **Compliance document set** — sub-processor disclosure, DPIA input sheet,
53	  breach-notification runbook, and counsel-gated DPA/BAA templates, published on the docs
54	  site.
55	- **Hardened containers** — the backend image now runs as a non-root user.
56	
57	- ⚠️ **Workspace roles — Admin / Member / Viewer (ADR 0033)** — authorization is now two
58	  axes. Your **workspace role** says what kind of user you are; the existing per-suite
59	  `view / edit / admin / owner` grants say what you can touch. Neither replaces the other:
60	  a Member with no share on a suite still cannot see it.
61	
62	  | Capability | Admin | Member | Viewer |
63	  |---|---|---|---|
64	  | See/use suites shared to them | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (view only) |
65	  | Create/import suites (become owner) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
66	  | Receive `edit` shares | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ — capped at `view` |
67	  | Connections: create / edit / delete / re-auth | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
68	  | Connections: list & reference in suites | ✅ | ✅ | list only |
69	  | Connections: test | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
70	  | `/admin`, implicit suite-admin, workspace-wide visibility | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
71	
72	  **BREAKING — Members lose connection-write.** Previously *any* authenticated user could
73	  delete or re-credential the connection every suite in the workspace ran on. If people who
74	  are not workspace admins manage connections in your deployment, **promote them to Admin
75	  before upgrading**, or those operations will start returning 403.
76	
77	  Everything else upgrades with **no config change**: existing users become Members (which
78	  is exactly what they could already do), and `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` keeps resolving to
79	  Admin — it is now a **bootstrap seed and lockout break-glass** rather than the admin
80	  mechanism, and it only ever grants, never demotes. New: `AUTH_OTP_DEFAULT_ROLE` /
81	  `AUTH_OIDC_DEFAULT_ROLE` set the tier new signups land on (`member` by default; set
82	  `viewer` when your signup allowlist is a whole domain).
83	
84	  Roles resolve **per request**, so a change takes effect on the target's next request —
85	  including requests made with their existing API tokens, which authenticate as their user.
86	  There is no token to revoke.
87	
88	- **Security hardening across both reference deployments** —
89	  ([#1386](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1386),
90	  [#1387](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1387),
91	  [#1388](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1388)):
92	  - **Who may hold an account is now an explicit decision.** DataQ provisions a user on first
93	    successful OIDC sign-in, so the identity provider's registration policy was in effect the
94	    product's access policy. The AWS reference pool is now admin-create-only, and a new
95	    app-side allowlist (`OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS` / `OIDC_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`) is enforced on every
96	    request — on REST **and** MCP — so it revokes as well as admits.
97	  - **Browser security headers on every response** — CSP, HSTS, `X-Frame-Options`,
98	    `nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy`. The CSP matters here because the UI
99	    renders warehouse-supplied content (failing-row samples, error text).
100	  - **Edge protection on AWS** — a CloudFront WAF per-IP rate ceiling in front of the in-app
101	    limiter (which fails open by design), plus edge caching of the fingerprinted bundle so
102	    the distribution actually absorbs load instead of passing everything through.
103	
104	- **AWS as a second deployment target** — a live-verified OpenTofu reference stack
105	  ([`deploy/terraform/aws/`](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/tree/main/deploy/terraform/aws)):
106	  ECS Fargate (api / worker / frontend) + RDS + ElastiCache + **Amazon Cognito** (via the
107	  same generic OIDC contract) + **AWS Secrets Manager** (`SECRET_STORE=aws_secrets_manager`,
108	  a fourth secret backend) behind **CloudFront** with an nginx-enforced origin secret;
109	  **SES email alerts**, **X-Ray tracing** through an ADOT sidecar on the app's
110	  vendor-neutral OTLP export, and a dedicated **Deploy (AWS)** GitHub Actions workflow.
111	  Azure remains the primary reference deployment.
112	- **dbt as a third orchestration provider** — observe dbt builds and trigger suites on
113	  success, via a post-build HMAC callback + a `run_results.json` artifact poll (ADR 0029).
114	- **Apache Iceberg as a fifth datasource** — native `pyiceberg` read (v2 baseline; ADR
115	  0030, #716/#722), with natively-computed freshness/volume monitors, a column profiler +
116	  column listing, and dry-run preview (#721).
117	- **Freshness & volume monitors** — the first auto-monitor kinds (is the data stale? did the
118	  load land whole?) on SQL datasources plus Iceberg.
119	- **Vendor-neutral observability** — OpenTelemetry logs + traces, exportable to Application

    Use this for 'what are we connected to?', 'which connections are broken?', or
    to find the connection a suite should run against. Returns, per connection:
    its id, name, type (``snowflake`` / ``adls_gen2`` / ``s3`` / ``unity_catalog``
    / ``iceberg`` for datasources; ``adf`` / ``airflow`` / ``dbt`` for
    orchestration providers), environment, whether a credential is stored, and
    its health — when it was last polled or last ran, a classified error reason
    when it is failing, how many consecutive failures it has had, and when its
    credential expires if the credential states a lifetime. Optionally filter by
    ``type`` or ``env``.

    **Read ``consecutive_run_failures`` narrowly.** It is non-zero only when
    *every* suite running on the connection is currently failing — the shape a
    dead credential has — and it is then the smallest such streak across those
    suites, capped at the last 20 runs each. A single succeeding suite resets it
    to 0 and clears the error even while another suite on the same connection
    fails every run, so a per-suite problem is invisible here; use
    ``list_runs(suite_id=…)`` for that.

    **Deliberately excludes every connection's configuration.** Names, types and
    health are what a question about connections needs; account identifiers,
    hosts, paths and secret references are not, and this is the surface where
    they would be handed to a model verbatim. Read a connection's config in the
    app if you need it.

    A null health timestamp means *unknown* — nothing has polled or run yet —
    never "healthy", and ``consecutive_run_failures`` is likewise null rather
    than 0 for a connection that has never run. A null ``credential_expires_at``
    means either that this credential type states no readable lifetime **or**
    that its expiry has never been read — ``credential_expiry_checked_at`` tells
    the two apart, and null there means we have never looked. Report all of these
    as silence rather than reassurance.
    """
    if type is not None and type not in CONNECTION_TYPES:
        raise ToolError(f"type must be one of {list(CONNECTION_TYPES)}")

        # and MCP has no connection-write tool at all, since a credential must
        # never transit an LLM (#529's standing exclusion).
        conns = connection_service.list_connections(session, conn_type=type, env=env)
        # One batched query for the whole list, not one per connection (#947).
        health = connection_service.datasource_health(session, [c.id for c in conns])

2378	    """Check whether a stored connection can actually reach its datasource.
2379	
2380	    Use this for 'is the Snowflake connection working?' or when a run has failed
2381	    and you need to tell a dead credential from a broken check. Opens a live
2382	    connection using the stored credential and reports success or a failure.
2383	
2384	    **What a pass proves is narrow:** the credential authenticates and the
2385	    datasource answers a trivial query. It does **not** check that a suite's
2386	    target table exists, that the role can read it, or that the run
2387	    configuration is complete — a connection can pass here and fail every suite
2388	    run (a Snowflake connection with no Role does exactly that). An ``ok: true``
2389	    beside a failing run means "not a dead credential", not "the connection is
2390	    fine".
2391	
2392	    A failure is deliberately **unclassified**: the driver's own message can
2393	    carry DSN and credential fragments, so it is withheld. Do not speculate
2394	    about the cause — report that the probe failed and that the server logs
2395	    carry the detail.
2396	
2397	    Nothing is changed and no credential is ever returned — this reports only
2398	    whether the probe worked. Requires the **member** workspace role: it spends a
2399	    stored credential against a remote system, which is not something a read-only
2400	    Viewer does. Fixing a failing connection (re-auth, edit, delete) is
2401	    Admin-only and is deliberately not available here at all — a credential must
2402	    never pass through an AI assistant.
2403	    """
2404	    cid = _parse_uuid(connection_id, field="connection_id")
2405	    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
2406	        # The coarse axis: a connection has no suite, so there is no resource
2407	        # ladder to ride and `require_permission` has nothing to gate on. This is
2408	        # what `_require_role` exists for, and it mirrors the REST route's
2409	        # `MemberUser` exactly (ADR 0033's matrix puts `test` at Member+ while
2410	        # every connection *mutation* is Admin-only).
2411	        _require_role(user, DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ROLE)
2412	        connection = connection_service.get_connection(session, cid)
2413	        connection_service.test_connection(session, cid, secret_store=get_secret_store())
2414	        return {
2415	            "connection_id": connection_id,
2416	            "name": connection.name,
2417	            "type": connection.type,
2418	            "env": connection.env,
2419	            "ok": True,

    and you need to tell a dead credential from a broken check. Opens a live
    connection using the stored credential and reports success or a failure.

    **What a pass proves is narrow:** the credential authenticates and the
    datasource answers a trivial query. It does **not** check that a suite's
    target table exists, that the role can read it, or that the run
    configuration is complete — a connection can pass here and fail every suite
    run (a Snowflake connection with no Role does exactly that). An ``ok: true``
    beside a failing run means "not a dead credential", not "the connection is
    fine".

    A failure is deliberately **unclassified**: the driver's own message can
    carry DSN and credential fragments, so it is withheld. Do not speculate
    about the cause — report that the probe failed and that the server logs
    carry the detail.

    whether the probe worked. Requires the **member** workspace role: it spends a
    stored credential against a remote system, which is not something a read-only
    Viewer does. Fixing a failing connection (re-auth, edit, delete) is
    Admin-only and is deliberately not available here at all — a credential must
    never pass through an AI assistant.

list_connections claimed a "classified error reason" while test_connection
said a failure is "deliberately unclassified" — neither cross-referenced
the other, so an investigating model could quote a classified reason from
one tool while telling the user the other cannot classify. Both docstrings
now name what "classified" means and point at each other: list_connections
reports a stored, classified reason from the last real run/poll;
test_connection performs a live probe with no reason at all.

Docstring-only change, no behavior change. mcp-honesty-reviewer verified
the added text against the actual code paths (failure_classifier's closed
taxonomy vs. ConnectionTestFailedError's fixed unclassified message).

def create_check(
    suite_id: str,
    name: str,
    expectation_type: str,
    config: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    kind: str = "expectation",
    warn_threshold: float | None = None,
    fail_threshold: float | None = None,
    critical_threshold: float | None = None,
    source_connection_id: str | None = None,
    dimension: str | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite.

    Use this for 'add a null check on email to the customer suite'. ``name`` is a
    human label; ``expectation_type`` is a GX expectation (e.g.
    ``expect_column_values_to_not_be_null``); ``config`` carries its arguments
    (e.g. ``{"column": "email"}``). Optional warn/fail/critical thresholds band
    the result severity. For a cross-dataset reconciliation check use
    ``kind="comparison"`` with ``expectation_type="comparison:records"``,
    ``source_connection_id`` (the baseline connection to compare against) and a

def update_check(
    suite_id: str,
    check_id: str,
    name: str | None = None,
    expectation_type: str | None = None,
    config: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    warn_threshold: float | None = None,
    fail_threshold: float | None = None,
    critical_threshold: float | None = None,
    dimension: str | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Change an existing check's definition — a partial update.

    Use this for 'loosen the null check on email to warn at 2%' or 'rename that
    check'. Omitted **arguments** are left as they were.

    ``config`` is the exception, and it matters: passing it **replaces the whole
    configuration**, it does not merge into it. So to change one setting you must
    send the complete config with that one setting altered — read the check first
    with ``get_check`` and edit what you get back. Sending only the key you want
    to change silently drops every other key: raising ``max_value`` on a
    between-check by sending ``{"max_value": 100}`` deletes its ``min_value``, and
    because the result is still a valid check it saves and reports success.

    Because omission means "leave alone", there is **no way to clear a field back
    to empty** through this tool. Say so rather than passing 0 or an empty string,
    which would set that value, not clear it. If an earlier version of the check
    had the field empty, ``restore_check_version`` will clear it — that is the
    one path that applies emptiness rather than skipping it; otherwise the check
    must be recreated. ``kind`` cannot be changed at all; recreate the check as
    the other kind.

    Every update snapshots the new state as a check version, so the change is
    reviewable with ``list_check_versions`` and reversible with
    ``restore_check_version``. Requires edit access to the suite.
    """
    sid = _parse_uuid(suite_id, field="suite_id")
    cid = _parse_uuid(check_id, field="check_id")
    _reject_nul(
        name=name or "",
        expectation_type=expectation_type or "",
        kind="",
        config=config or {},
        dimension=dimension or "",
    )
    with _ctx() as (session, user), _service_errors():
        require_permission(session, sid, user.id, minimum="edit")
        check = check_service.update_check(
            session,
            sid,
            cid,
            name=name,
            expectation_type=expectation_type,
            config=config,
            warn_threshold=_dec(warn_threshold),
            fail_threshold=_dec(fail_threshold),
            critical_threshold=_dec(critical_threshold),
            dimension=dimension,
            actor_id=user.id,
        )
        return _check_summary(check)

content.text:
Confirmed docstring-only, single file. Now let's finalize the review report.

---

## Part A — Findings

**🔴 Silent honesty gap — `create_check`, the `volume` monitor sampling claim (criterion: False docstrings, not just thin ones)**

The diff adds:

> "``volume`` (row count vs ``min_rows``/``max_rows`` — **on ADLS / S3 / Iceberg targets this counts a capped sample, not the full file**, so a `volume` check there bounds sample size, not table size)"

This is false. I traced the actual `volume` monitor-kind execution path on both affected datasource families:

- `backend/app/datasources/flatfile.py::FlatFileCheckRunner.run_monitors` (shared by `adls_gen2` and `s3` — confirmed via `registry.py`'s builder table) computes `rows()` via the full `row_count()` helper (streaming count, not `read_sampled_dataframe`) unless another monitor in the same call also needs the dataframe, in which case it uses `len(dataframe())` off the **unsampled** `read_dataframe`. Neither path ever calls `read_sampled_dataframe`/`self._sampling`.
- `backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py::IcebergCheckRunner._monitor_scalar` for `VOLUME` reads the Iceberg snapshot-summary metadata (a true full-table count) or falls back to `table.scan().count()` — again a full count, never a sample.
- Most tellingly, `backend/app/datasources/sampling.py`'s own `SAMPLING_ROW_COUNT_CONFLICT` message — the exact sentence `check_service.create_check` raises when a row-count *expectation* is paired with a sampled suite — says in the codebase's own words: *"Use a volume monitor, which counts the whole dataset without loading it, or drop the sampling block from the suite's run target."* The `volume` monitor kind exists specifically **because** it gives the true, unsampled count, which is the opposite of what the new docstring claims.

The wrong answer this produces: an LLM reading this docstring would tell a user "your `volume` check on that S3 target is only checking a sample, the alert doesn't reflect the true row count" — which is backwards. The actual caveat that *does* exist (a `kind="expectation"`, `expect_table_row_count_to_be_between` check measuring the sample) is a different code path entirely, already covered by `_reject_row_count_on_sampled_suite`, and is not what `kind="volume"`/`min_rows`/`max_rows` refers to. This looks like the caveat was carried over from `dryrun_check`'s neighboring docstring (which discusses a "volume preview" in the context of GX row-count expectations under `_load_frame`'s sampling) and misapplied to the monitor kind of the same name.

This must be fixed before merge — it recreates exactly the class of defect (a confident, specific, wrong claim) the PR is meant to close, on the very PR meant to close it.

**✅ Verified accurate — claims 1, 3, 4, 5**

- Claim 1 (config validated against GX schema only): confirmed — `validate_expectation_check` in `backend/app/services/check_service.py:557-590` only instantiates the GX `Expectation` pydantic model with the config; there is no column-existence/datasource introspection anywhere in `create_check`'s validation chain for the ordinary-expectation path.
- Claim 3 (anomaly `min_points`/`seasonality` semantics): confirmed against `backend/app/services/anomaly.py` — `build_score_payload` sets `insufficient_history`/`skip` when `len(priors) < params.min_points`, and `eligible_values` filters priors to `o.ts.weekday() == now.weekday()` when `seasonality=True`, exactly "compare against the same day-of-week."
- Claim 4 (`dimension: null` = unclassified, not failed): confirmed — `backend/app/services/asset_view_service.py` builds `checks_by_dimension` filtering `if d is not None`, and unclassified checks land in `uncovered = sorted(set(DQ_DIMENSIONS) - set(checks_by_dimension))`, i.e. a coverage gap, never an error path.
- Claim 5 (create doesn't run it): confirmed — `check_service.create_check` (backend/app/services/check_service.py:624-723) only inserts the `Check` row, records a version, audits, and commits; no dispatch/run call anywhere in the function or in the MCP tool wrapper.

**🟡 Disclosed-but-buried — ordering (summary → returns → caveats)**

The final line — "Requires edit access. Returns the created check's id." — is placed after four stacked bolded caveats (config validation, volume sampling, dimension null semantics, no-auto-run). Per the standing rule recorded in CLAUDE.md from the 2026-08-17 honesty pass ("summary → what it returns → caveats... pushing the 'Returns…' contract below [a caveat] makes selection harder without making the caveat more likely to be read"), the contract statement should be pulled up near the top, right after the opening summary, with caveats following it. This is a real but lower-severity finding — it doesn't produce a wrong answer, just risks the same ordering regression already once caught and fixed on this exact surface.

**Inert parameters:** none — docstring-only diff, no parameters added/changed.

**Serialization risk:** none — no code touched.

**Neighbour staleness:** none found. Grepped the modified docstring text against the standard "in the app"/"no way to"/etc. phrases — no hits, and this PR adds no new capability, so it can't retroactively falsify a sibling's "go do X in the app" sentence. `dryrun_check`'s pre-existing "volume preview" caveat (line ~1936-1945) is about a different code path (GX row-count expectations under suite-level sampling via `_load_frame`) and is not itself touched or newly contradicted by this diff — but see the note below.

**Related, not introduced by this diff, worth flagging while here:** `dryrun_check`'s own docstring line "a `volume` preview's row count is not the file's row count" is ambiguous in the same way the new text is wrong — `dry_run_service.dry_run_check` (backend/app/services/dryrun_service.py:87-92) raises `DryRunUnsupportedError` for any `kind` other than `expectation`/`schema_drift`/`anomaly`, meaning `kind="volume"` **cannot be dry-run at all**. If that sentence is intended to describe the monitor `volume` kind, it's unreachable code paths being described as behavior. If it's intended to describe a GX `expect_table_row_count_to_be_between` *expectation* check (colloquially "a volume preview"), the wording is at minimum confusing next to `create_check`'s new, more precise "volume" (monitor-kind) language, and worth disambiguating in a follow-up. Not blocking this PR, but flag/file it — the same ambiguity that just produced a false claim in `create_check` is sitting unaddressed in its neighbor.

## Part B — generic MCP-quality observations (advisory)

- **Tool-selection honesty**: first sentence of `create_check` ("Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite.") is unchanged by this diff and already disambiguates fine against `update_check`/`dryrun_check`. No issue.
- **Confidence/derived-value framing**: the new anomaly z-score explanation ("this is not a value the metric itself will ever reach, so do not treat it like a domain threshold") is a good example of exactly this Part B check being satisfied proactively — no finding.
- **Error-path actionability**: not applicable, no new `ToolError` paths in this diff.
- **Unit/format ambiguity, silent input coercion**: not applicable, no parameters changed.

## Verdict

`Block — 1 silent honesty gap (the #1444/#1449 shape). The claim "on ADLS / S3 / Iceberg targets this counts a capped sample, not the full file" for the `volume` monitor kind is false — the code (and the codebase's own `SAMPLING_ROW_COUNT_CONFLICT` message) shows the opposite: the volume monitor exists specifically to give the true unsampled count. Fix that sentence (or remove it) before merge. Also move the "Returns the created check's id" contract sentence up nearer the summary per the standing ordering rule (🟡, non-blocking but should be fixed in the same PR since it's trivial). All four other new claims (config-validation-only, anomaly min_points/seasonality, dimension-null-as-coverage-gap, no-auto-run-on-create) were verified accurate against the implementation.`

input.title: MCP: dryrun_check's "volume preview" caveat describes an unreachable kind
input.body:
Found by the `mcp-honesty-reviewer` agent while fixing #1448 (`create_check` caveats, PR TBD).

## The issue

`dryrun_check`'s docstring says:

> "a `volume` preview's row count is not the file's row count [on ADLS/S3/Iceberg, under suite-level sampling]"

But `dry_run_service.dry_run_check` (`backend/app/services/dryrun_service.py`) raises `DryRunUnsupportedError` for any `kind` other than `expectation`/`schema_drift`/`anomaly` — so `kind="volume"` **cannot be dry-run at all**. The sentence describes a code path that cannot execute.

Two readings, both problematic:

1. If it's meant to describe the monitor `volume` kind: that kind can't reach `dryrun_check`, so the caveat is dead text about unreachable behavior.
2. If it's meant to describe an ordinary GX `expect_table_row_count_to_be_between` *expectation* check under a sampled suite's `_load_frame`: that's a real and correct caveat, but calling it "a `volume` preview" is confusing now that `create_check`'s docstring (#1448) uses "volume" specifically to mean the `kind="volume"` monitor, which — unlike the expectation — counts the true dataset size on every datasource, samples included.

The two "volume"s now mean opposite things in neighboring docstrings on the same file, which is exactly the class of defect #1448 was about.

## Fix

Disambiguate the `dryrun_check` sentence: either drop "volume" as a label entirely and describe the row-count-under-sampling case in expectation-specific terms, or rename to make clear it's about `expect_table_row_count_to_be_between`, not `kind="volume"`.

## Acceptance

- [ ] `dryrun_check`'s docstring no longer uses "volume preview" to describe a code path it cannot reach
- [ ] The real caveat (row-count expectation under a sampled suite) is stated in terms that don't collide with the `kind="volume"` monitor's meaning elsewhere in the file

content.text:
Both referenced tools exist. Verdict below.

## Findings

**Volume sentence — CONFIRMED ACCURATE.**
`backend/app/datasources/sampling.py:51` (`SAMPLING_ROW_COUNT_CONFLICT`) states a volume monitor "counts the whole dataset without loading it." `backend/app/datasources/flatfile.py:712-726` backs this for ADLS/S3: the `VOLUME` branch calls `row_count()` (Parquet footer / CSV stream, `flatfile.py:364-371`), never `dataframe()`/`read_dataframe()`, and the latter's own docstring says "Checks need every row/column — counts must be exact." `backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py:306-330` backs it for Iceberg: `VOLUME` reads `_volume_from_snapshot_summary(table)`, Iceberg's own metadata-level total-records count, not a sampled read. The corrected sentence — "this counts the true dataset size on every datasource, including ADLS / S3 / Iceberg, unlike an ordinary row-count *expectation* check on a sampled suite, which measures the sample" — is now true and correctly distinguishes the monitor-kind path from the sampled-suite expectation path (`ROW_COUNT_EXPECTATION_TYPES` in `sampling.py:41-46`, which is exactly what *does* get refused/measures-the-sample). Good fix.

**Opening sentence — satisfies the ordering rule.**
"Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite. Requires edit access to the suite. Returns the created check's id." is summary → gate → returns, all in sentence one, with every caveat (config-not-validated, dimension-null semantics, doesn't-run-on-create) now following in body paragraphs. This matches the summary→returns→caveats convention. Reads well; no redundant restatement at the end anymore.

**Other issues found on a fresh full re-read — none blocking, two minor pre-existing (not introduced by this diff, not worth a new finding):**
- The return dict actually includes `id`, `suite_id`, `name`, `expectation_type`, `dimension` (`backend/app/mcp/server.py:1728-1734`), so "Returns the created check's id" is an understatement of the payload, not a false claim (returning more than promised is not a Part-A honesty defect — a caller getting extra true fields cannot be misled). Wording is unchanged from the pre-diff docstring, just relocated — not a regression from this PR.
- The `comparison` paragraph names only `comparison:records`; `COMPARISON_EXPECTATION_TYPES` in `check_service.py:73` also accepts `comparison:columns`. This sentence is verbatim pre-existing text, untouched by this diff (confirmed via `git diff` — it was only moved, not edited), so it's not a defect introduced by the change under review and outside this targeted re-verification's scope.
- Anomaly config fields (`target_metric`, `column`, `window`, `min_points`, `seasonality`) all check out against `backend/app/datasources/monitors.py:316-387` — accurate, unchanged content, just reformatted into a bulleted list for readability.

## Verdict

Pass — both fixes verified correct (volume sentence accurate against `flatfile.py`/`iceberg.py`/`sampling.py`; opening sentence satisfies summary→returns→caveats). No new honesty defects found on the full fresh re-read of the current docstring. Ready to merge.

Context: an earlier review pass on this same diff found the sentence "on ADLS / S3 / Iceberg targets this counts a capped sample, not the full file" (about the `volume` monitor kind) was FALSE — the volume monitor kind gives a true unsampled count on every datasource, confirmed against `backend/app/datasources/flatfile.py`, `backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py`, and the `SAMPLING_ROW_COUNT_CONFLICT` message in `backend/app/datasources/sampling.py`. 1. The volume sentence now reads: "``volume`` (row count vs ``min_rows``/``max_rows`` — this counts the true dataset size on every datasource, including ADLS / S3 / Iceberg, unlike an ordinary row-count *expectation* check on a sampled suite, which measures the sample)"
2. The docstring's first line now reads: "Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite. Requires edit access to the suite. Returns the created check's id." — with the redundant trailing sentence removed from the end.

Please verify:
- Is the corrected volume sentence now accurate? (Re-confirm against the same files if needed.)
- Does the new opening sentence read well and satisfy the ordering rule?
- Any other issues in the full current docstring (re-read the whole function's docstring fresh, not just the two changed spots) — this is the final check before merge.

Keep the report concise — this is a targeted re-verification of a known fix, not a full fresh audit.

content.text:
Both referenced tools exist. Verdict below.

## Findings

**Volume sentence — CONFIRMED ACCURATE.**
`backend/app/datasources/sampling.py:51` (`SAMPLING_ROW_COUNT_CONFLICT`) states a volume monitor "counts the whole dataset without loading it." `backend/app/datasources/flatfile.py:712-726` backs this for ADLS/S3: the `VOLUME` branch calls `row_count()` (Parquet footer / CSV stream, `flatfile.py:364-371`), never `dataframe()`/`read_dataframe()`, and the latter's own docstring says "Checks need every row/column — counts must be exact." `backend/app/datasources/iceberg.py:306-330` backs it for Iceberg: `VOLUME` reads `_volume_from_snapshot_summary(table)`, Iceberg's own metadata-level total-records count, not a sampled read. The corrected sentence — "this counts the true dataset size on every datasource, including ADLS / S3 / Iceberg, unlike an ordinary row-count *expectation* check on a sampled suite, which measures the sample" — is now true and correctly distinguishes the monitor-kind path from the sampled-suite expectation path (`ROW_COUNT_EXPECTATION_TYPES` in `sampling.py:41-46`, which is exactly what *does* get refused/measures-the-sample). Good fix.

**Opening sentence — satisfies the ordering rule.**
"Add a new check (a Great Expectations expectation) to a suite. Requires edit access to the suite. Returns the created check's id." is summary → gate → returns, all in sentence one, with every caveat (config-not-validated, dimension-null semantics, doesn't-run-on-create) now following in body paragraphs. This matches the summary→returns→caveats convention. Reads well; no redundant restatement at the end anymore.

**Other issues found on a fresh full re-read — none blocking, two minor pre-existing (not introduced by this diff, not worth a new finding):**
- The return dict actually includes `id`, `suite_id`, `name`, `expectation_type`, `dimension` (`backend/app/mcp/server.py:1728-1734`), so "Returns the created check's id" is an understatement of the payload, not a false claim (returning more than promised is not a Part-A honesty defect — a caller getting extra true fields cannot be misled). Wording is unchanged from the pre-diff docstring, just relocated — not a regression from this PR.
- The `comparison` paragraph names only `comparison:records`; `COMPARISON_EXPECTATION_TYPES` in `check_service.py:73` also accepts `comparison:columns`. This sentence is verbatim pre-existing text, untouched by this diff (confirmed via `git diff` — it was only moved, not edited), so it's not a defect introduced by the change under review and outside this targeted re-verification's scope.
- Anomaly config fields (`target_metric`, `column`, `window`, `min_points`, `seasonality`) all check out against `backend/app/datasources/monitors.py:316-387` — accurate, unchanged content, just reformatted into a bulleted list for readability.

## Verdict

Pass — both fixes verified correct (volume sentence accurate against `flatfile.py`/`iceberg.py`/`sampling.py`; opening sentence satisfies summary→returns→caveats). No new honesty defects found on the full fresh re-read of the current docstring. Ready to merge.

- `create_check` was a dense parameter reference with essentially no honesty fields, in a catalog that treats them seriously everywhere else.

## Linked issue
Fixes #1448.

## Type of change
- [x] docs — documentation only

## Checklist
- [x] Manually tested locally (`pytest backend/tests/mcp` — 234 passed)
- [x] Single functionality — no unrelated changes piggybacked
- [x] Conventional commit title
- [x] No secrets, credentials, or `.env` files committed

- [x] `docs/progress.md` — N/A
- [x] Security implications considered — none, docstring-only

## Schema migration?
- [x] No schema change

## Manual test notes
`pytest backend/tests/mcp` (234 passed). Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit clean.

## Security / risk notes
None — docstring-only. Worth flagging for reviewers: the first `mcp-honesty-reviewer` pass caught a real overclaim in my draft — I'd written that the `volume` monitor kind sample-caps on ADLS/S3/Iceberg, which is backwards (it gives the true unsampled count; verified against `flatfile.py`/`iceberg.py`/`sampling.py`'s own `SAMPLING_ROW_COUNT_CONFLICT` message). Fixed and re-verified by a second pass. Filed #1592 for a related, out-of-scope ambiguity the same review surfaced in `dryrun_check`'s own "volume preview" wording.

    *,
    name: str,
    expectation_type: str,
    kind: str,
    config: dict[str, Any],
    dimension: str = "",
) -> None:

@mcp.tool
def get_adf_pipeline_status(
    provider: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None,
    limit: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=200)] = 20,
    offset: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)] = 0,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Get recent orchestration pipeline/DAG runs with their correlated DQ result.

    Use this for 'why did the customer pipeline fail?'. Returns the most recent
    ADF / Airflow / dbt pipeline runs —
    provider, pipeline/DAG id, run status, start/end times — and, when a DQ suite
    was triggered by that pipeline run (and is visible to the user), the triggered
    run's id and status. Optionally filter by ``provider`` ('adf', 'airflow' or
    'dbt') and/or ``status``.

    **There is no time filter**, so "did anything fail overnight?" cannot be
    asked directly: this returns the ``limit`` most recent runs, and
    ``oldest_in_page`` says how far back you actually saw. If ``oldest_in_page``
    is later than the window you were asked about, you have not seen the whole
    window — raise ``limit`` or page with ``offset``, and say so rather than
    answering "nothing failed".

    Only pipelines DataQ has ingested appear here. A short or empty result can
    also mean no orchestration connection is configured for that provider and
    environment, or that its poller is failing — check ``list_connections``
    before reporting an all-clear.
    """
    # All three orchestration providers (ADR 0029 added dbt), from the shared
    # vocabulary. The old two-name literal rejected `dbt` — the obvious next call
    # after `list_trigger_bindings(provider="dbt")` returns a dbt binding.
    if provider is not None and provider not in ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS:
        raise ToolError(f"provider must be one of {list(ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS)}")
    if status is not None and status not in PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES:
        # An unvalidated status would return `[]`, which reads as "no pipeline
        # failed" on the one question this tool exists to answer (#828).
        raise ToolError(f"status must be one of {list(PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES)}")
    with _ctx() as (session, user):
        total = orchestration_service.count_pipeline_runs(session, provider=provider, status=status)
        runs = orchestration_service.list_pipeline_runs(
            session, provider=provider, status=status, limit=limit, offset=offset
        )
        accessible = set(
            session.scalars(
                suite_service.accessible_suite_ids(user.id, include_all=is_workspace_admin(user))
            )
        )
        out: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
        for pr in runs:
            marker = f"{pr.provider}:{pr.pipeline_or_dag_id}:{pr.provider_run_id}"
            dq = session.scalars(
                select(Run).where(Run.triggered_by == marker).order_by(Run.created_at.desc())
            ).first()
            correlated = (
                {"run_id": str(dq.id), "status": dq.status}
                if dq is not None and dq.suite_id in accessible
                else None
            )
            out.append(
                {
                    "provider": pr.provider,
                    "pipeline": pr.pipeline_or_dag_id,
                    "status": pr.status,
                    "started_at": pr.started_at.isoformat() if pr.started_at else None,
                    "finished_at": pr.finished_at.isoformat() if pr.finished_at else None,
                    "dq_run": correlated,
                    # Distinguishes "no suite was triggered" from "a suite was
                    # triggered and you cannot see it" — the same fact the
                    # docstring stated in prose and the payload conflated.
                    "dq_run_restricted": dq is not None and dq.suite_id not in accessible,
                }
            )
        return {
            "total": total,
            "returned": len(out),
            "truncated": offset + len(out) < total,
            **_page_window([pr.started_at or pr.created_at for pr in runs]),
            "pipeline_runs": out,
        }

@mcp.tool
def get_adf_pipeline_status(
    provider: str | None = None,
    status: str | None = None,
    limit: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1, le=200)] = 20,
    offset: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)] = 0,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Get recent orchestration pipeline/DAG runs with their correlated DQ result.

    Use this for 'why did the customer pipeline fail?'. Returns the most recent
    ADF / Airflow / dbt pipeline runs —
    provider, pipeline/DAG id, run status, start/end times — and, when a DQ suite
    was triggered by that pipeline run (and is visible to the user), the triggered
    run's id and status. Optionally filter by ``provider`` ('adf', 'airflow' or
    'dbt') and/or ``status``.

    **There is no time filter**, so "did anything fail overnight?" cannot be
    asked directly: this returns the ``limit`` most recent runs, and
    ``oldest_in_page`` says how far back you actually saw. If ``oldest_in_page``
    is later than the window you were asked about, you have not seen the whole
    window — raise ``limit`` or page with ``offset``, and say so rather than
    answering "nothing failed".

    Only pipelines DataQ has ingested appear here. A short or empty result can
    also mean no orchestration connection is configured for that provider and
    environment, or that its poller is failing — check ``list_connections``
    before reporting an all-clear.
    """
    # All three orchestration providers (ADR 0029 added dbt), from the shared
    # vocabulary. The old two-name literal rejected `dbt` — the obvious next call
    # after `list_trigger_bindings(provider="dbt")` returns a dbt binding.
    if provider is not None and provider not in ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS:
        raise ToolError(f"provider must be one of {list(ORCHESTRATION_PROVIDERS)}")
    if status is not None and status not in PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES:
        # An unvalidated status would return `[]`, which reads as "no pipeline
        # failed" on the one question this tool exists to answer (#828).
        raise ToolError(f"status must be one of {list(PIPELINE_RUN_STATUSES)}")
    with _ctx() as (session, user):
        total = orchestration_service.count_pipeline_runs(session, provider=provider, status=status)
        runs = orchestration_service.list_pipeline_runs(
            session, provider=provider, status=status, limit=limit, offset=offset
        )
        accessible = set(
            session.scalars(
                suite_service.accessible_suite_ids(user.id, include_all=is_workspace_admin(user))
            )
        )
        out: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
        for pr in runs:
            marker = f"{pr.provider}:{pr.pipeline_or_dag_id}:{pr.provider_run_id}"
            dq = session.scalars(
                select(Run).where(Run.triggered_by == marker).order_by(Run.created_at.desc())
            ).first()
            correlated = (
                {"run_id": str(dq.id), "status": dq.status}
                if dq is not None and dq.suite_id in accessible
                else None
            )
            out.append(
                {
                    "provider": pr.provider,
                    "pipeline": pr.pipeline_or_dag_id,
                    "status": pr.status,
                    "started_at": pr.started_at.isoformat() if pr.started_at else None,
                    "finished_at": pr.finished_at.isoformat() if pr.finished_at else None,
                    "dq_run": correlated,
                    # Distinguishes "no suite was triggered" from "a suite was
                    # triggered and you cannot see it" — the same fact the
                    # docstring stated in prose and the payload conflated.
                    "dq_run_restricted": dq is not None and dq.suite_id not in accessible,
                }
            )
        return {
            "total": total,
            "returned": len(out),
            "truncated": offset + len(out) < total,
            **_page_window([pr.started_at or pr.created_at for pr in runs]),
            "pipeline_runs": out,
        }

            dq = session.scalars(
                select(Run).where(Run.triggered_by == marker).order_by(Run.created_at.desc())
            ).first()
            correlated = (
                {"run_id": str(dq.id), "status": dq.status}
                if dq is not None and dq.suite_id in accessible
                else None
            )
            out.append(
                {
                    "provider": pr.provider,
                    "pipeline": pr.pipeline_or_dag_id,
                    "status": pr.status,
                    "started_at": pr.started_at.isoformat() if pr.started_at else None,
                    "finished_at": pr.finished_at.isoformat() if pr.finished_at else None,
                    "dq_run": correlated,
                    # Distinguishes "no suite was triggered" from "a suite was
                    # triggered and you cannot see it" — the same fact the
                    # docstring stated in prose and the payload conflated.
                    "dq_run_restricted": dq is not None and dq.suite_id not in accessible,
                }
            )
        return {
            "total": total,
            "returned": len(out),
            "truncated": offset + len(out) < total,
            **_page_window([pr.started_at or pr.created_at for pr in runs]),
            "pipeline_runs": out,
        }

"""The declared authorization gate of every MCP tool — one table, four sweeps."""

from __future__ import annotations

#: Tool name → its declared authorization gate. Keep alphabetical within a group.
GATES: dict[str, str] = {
    # ── no per-resource gate ───────────────────────────────────────────────── `list_assets` and
    # `get_asset` are here by ADR 0037's explicit decision.
    "get_adf_pipeline_status": "read",
    "get_asset": "read",
    "get_health_score": "read",
    "get_suite_performance": "read",
    "list_assets": "read",
    "list_connections": "read",
    "list_suites": "read",
    # ── accessible-suite scoped, and view-gated when a suite is named ────────
    "get_near_misses": "read:suite-optional",
    "list_incidents": "read:suite-optional",
    "list_runs": "read:suite-optional",
    "list_schedules": "read:suite-optional",
    "list_trigger_bindings": "read:suite-optional",
    # ── reads gated on the suite ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    "export_suite": "suite:view",
    "get_check": "suite:view",
    "get_check_history": "suite:view",
    "get_column_policy": "suite:view",
    "get_notification_config": "suite:view",
    "get_run_results": "suite:view",
    "get_run_status": "suite:view",
    "get_suite_results": "suite:view",
    "list_check_versions": "suite:view",
    "list_checks": "suite:view",
    # ── writes (and live probes) gated on the suite ────────────────────────── `profile_column` is
    # here, not with the reads: it persists nothing.
    "cancel_run": "suite:edit",
    "create_check": "suite:edit",
    "create_schedule": "suite:edit",
    "create_trigger_binding": "suite:edit",
    "delete_check": "suite:edit",
    "dryrun_check": "suite:edit",
    "list_columns": "suite:edit",
    "delete_schedule": "suite:edit",
    "delete_trigger_binding": "suite:edit",
    "profile_column": "suite:edit",
    "restore_check_version": "suite:edit",
    "set_column_policy": "suite:edit",
    "suggest_column_policy": "suite:edit",
    "snooze_check": "suite:edit",
    "trigger_suite_run": "suite:edit",
    "update_check": "suite:edit",
    "update_schedule": "suite:edit",
    "update_suite": "suite:edit",
    "update_trigger_binding": "suite:edit",
    # ── incident-scoped, via the incident's suite ────────────────────────────
    "ack_incident": "incident:edit",
    "get_incident": "incident:view",
    "resolve_incident": "incident:edit",
    # ── workspace-role gated: no suite to hang a resource gate on ─────────── `test_connection`
    # spends a stored credential against a remote system; `import_suite` CREATES a suite.
    "import_suite": "role:member",
    "test_connection": "role:member",
}

#: Gates whose tools must refuse a **Viewer**.
VIEWER_DENIED_GATES = frozenset({"suite:edit", "incident:edit", "role:member", "role:admin"})

#: Gates whose tools must refuse a **Member** — admin-only capabilities.
MEMBER_DENIED_GATES = frozenset({"role:admin"})

#: Gates whose tools must refuse a user with **no share on the named suite**.
OUTSIDER_DENIED_GATES = frozenset(
    {"suite:view", "suite:edit", "incident:view", "incident:edit", "read:suite-optional"}
)

#: Every value that may appear in `GATES`. A typo'd gate would otherwise silently
#: match no sweep and be enforced by nothing.
KNOWN_GATES = frozenset(
    {
        "read",
        "read:suite-optional",
        "suite:view",
        "suite:edit",
        "incident:view",
        "incident:edit",
        "role:member",
        "role:admin",
    }
)


def tools_with_gate(*gates: str) -> list[str]:
    """Tool names carrying any of `gates`, sorted for stable parametrize ids."""
    return sorted(name for name, gate in GATES.items() if gate in gates)


def viewer_denied_tools() -> list[str]:
    return tools_with_gate(*VIEWER_DENIED_GATES)


def member_denied_tools() -> list[str]:
    return tools_with_gate(*MEMBER_DENIED_GATES)


def outsider_denied_tools() -> list[str]:
    return tools_with_gate(*OUTSIDER_DENIED_GATES)

def test_get_pipeline_status_reports_truncation(db_session: Any, monkeypatch: Any) -> None:
    """It took `limit` and returned a bare list, so a full page was
    indistinguishable from the whole set on 'did any pipeline fail overnight?'.
    """
    user = _user(db_session)
    suite = _suite(db_session, user)
    _as(monkeypatch, db_session, user)
    for i in range(3):
        db_session.add(
            PipelineRun(
                provider="adf",
                connection_id=suite.connection_id,
                pipeline_or_dag_id=f"pl_{i}",
                provider_run_id=str(uuid.uuid4()),
                env="dev",
                status="succeeded",
            )
        )
    db_session.commit()

    page = server.get_pipeline_status(limit=2)
    assert page["total"] == 3
    assert page["truncated"] is True
    assert len(page["pipeline_runs"]) == 2

    with pytest.raises(ToolError):
        server.get_pipeline_status(status="explode")

## The 46 tools

Each tool is a thin wrapper over the same service layer as the REST API — per-suite
authorization (`view` for a read, `edit` for a mutation) and failing-sample redaction apply
identically. The 46 split three ways, not two:

- **23 read-only** — `export_suite`, `get_adf_pipeline_status`, `get_asset`, `get_check`,
  `get_check_history`, `get_column_policy`, `get_health_score`, `get_incident`,
  `get_near_misses`, `get_notification_config`, `get_run_results`, `get_run_status`,
  `get_suite_performance`, `get_suite_results`, `list_assets`, `list_check_versions`,
  `list_checks`, `list_connections`, `list_incidents`, `list_runs`, `list_schedules`,
  `list_suites`, `list_trigger_bindings`.
- **18 that change state** — `create_check`, `update_check`, `delete_check`, `snooze_check`,
  `restore_check_version`, `trigger_suite_run`, `cancel_run`, `update_suite`, `set_column_policy`,
  `create_schedule`, `update_schedule`, `delete_schedule`, `create_trigger_binding`,
  `update_trigger_binding`, `delete_trigger_binding`, `ack_incident`, `resolve_incident`,
  `import_suite`. All gate on `edit` access to the affected suite (the schedule, binding and
  incident tools via the suite they target); `import_suite` additionally requires the **member**
  workspace role, since it has no existing suite to gate on.
- **5 that persist nothing but open a live datasource connection using stored credentials** —
  `profile_column`, `list_columns`, `dryrun_check`, `suggest_column_policy`, `test_connection`.
  These are gated like writes, not like reads, because they spend a real credential against a
  remote system even though nothing is saved: the first four require `edit` on the suite whose
  connection they probe, and `test_connection` (which has no suite at all) requires the **member**
  workspace role.

No MCP tool is Admin-only. Every Admin-only capability in ADR 0033's authorization matrix is a
connection *mutation* (create/edit/delete/re-auth), and none of those are exposed here at all —
a credential must never transit an LLM. `test_connection` reports only whether a live probe
succeeded; it never returns a credential or a secret reference (Tier 1 + Tier 2 expansion, issue
[#529](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/529)).

### Reading the results honestly

attachment.snippet:
1	# AI assistants (MCP setup)
2	
3	DataQ ships a built-in [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server so AI assistants — Claude Desktop, Claude.ai, VS Code / GitHub Copilot, Cursor — can answer questions like *"what failed today?"* or *"run the orders suite"* against your live DataQ instance, with the same per-suite permissions as the signed-in user.
4	
5	## Endpoint & authentication
6	
7	The server is mounted on the deployed app at:
8	
9	```text
10	https://<your-dataq-host>/mcp/
11	```
12	
13	!!! warning "Keep the trailing slash"
14	    `/mcp` answers with a **307 redirect** to `/mcp/`, and some HTTP clients drop the
15	    `Authorization` header when following redirects — which then surfaces as a
16	    confusing 401. Always configure clients with the `/mcp/` form.
17	
18	The endpoint accepts the **same credentials as the REST API** (ADR [0008](adr/0008-mcp-server.md) / [0026](adr/0026-auth-api-keys-and-principal-seam.md)): an OIDC bearer token (Azure AD or Cognito), or a **DataQ API key** (`dq_live_…`). Without auth configured, the endpoint is only mounted in local dev-bypass mode — never unauthenticated in a deployed environment.
19	
20	!!! info "Email-OTP deployments: MCP works, with an API key"
21	    A deployment running **email one-time codes instead of SSO** (ADR
22	    [0032](adr/0032-email-otp-signin.md)) has no identity provider to issue bearer
23	    tokens, so an **API key is the only `/mcp` credential** there — mint one as
24	    below and use it exactly the same way. Everything else is identical, including
25	    all 46 tools and per-suite permissions. Two rejections are deliberate in that
26	    mode: a raw JWT is refused (there is nothing to validate it against), and your
27	    **sign-in session is never accepted** — it is a browser credential and does not
28	    authenticate `/mcp`, whether presented as a bearer or carried as a cookie.
29	
30	### Getting a token
31	
32	**Recommended — a DataQ API key (PAT):** mint one via `POST /api/v1/me/api-keys`
33	(see [API keys](api-keys.md)) and use it as the bearer. It lives up to a year,
34	is revocable per-integration, and runs with exactly your per-suite access —
35	built for always-on MCP configs.
36	
37	**Quick one-off — your web session's OIDC token:** sign in to the DataQ web
38	app, open your browser's developer tools → **Application → Session Storage** →
39	the `oidc.user:…` entry → copy the `access_token` value.
40	
41	!!! note "OIDC tokens expire after ~1 hour"
42	    The pasted browser token is short-lived; when the client starts getting
43	    401s, paste a fresh one and restart the MCP server/connection — or switch
44	    to an [API key](api-keys.md) and stop re-pasting.
45	
46	!!! danger "Never commit a config that carries a token"
47	    Keep token-bearing MCP config files out of version control (in the DataQ repo
48	    itself, `.gitignore` already covers `.vscode/*`).
49	
50	## Client configuration
51	
52	**Claude Desktop / Claude.ai** (`claude_desktop_config.json`) — and **GitHub Copilot** (`mcp.json`):
53	
54	```jsonc
55	{
56	  "mcpServers": {
57	    "dataq": {
58	      "url": "https://<your-dataq-host>/mcp/",
59	      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <AZURE_AD_ACCESS_TOKEN>" }
60	    }
61	  }
62	}
63	```
64	
65	**VS Code** (workspace `.vscode/mcp.json`, used by Copilot agent mode) uses a `servers` key — not `mcpServers` — plus an explicit `type`:
66	
67	```jsonc
68	{
69	  "servers": {
70	    "dataq": {
71	      "type": "http",
72	      "url": "https://<your-dataq-host>/mcp/",
73	      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer <AZURE_AD_ACCESS_TOKEN>" }
74	    }
75	  }
76	}
77	```
78	
79	Start it via the command palette (`Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P`) → **MCP: List Servers** → *dataq* → Start (or open Copilot Chat in agent mode — configured servers start on demand).
80	
81	**Cursor** (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`) uses the same `mcpServers` shape as Claude Desktop.
82	
83	## The 47 tools
84	
85	Each tool is a thin wrapper over the same service layer as the REST API — per-suite
86	authorization (`view` for a read, `edit` for a mutation) and failing-sample redaction apply
87	identically. The 47 split three ways, not two (one of the 24 reads, `get_adf_pipeline_status`,
88	is a deprecated alias kept only for backward compatibility — see below):
89	
90	- **24 read-only** — `export_suite`, `get_adf_pipeline_status` (deprecated, use
91	  `get_pipeline_status`), `get_asset`, `get_check`,
92	  `get_check_history`, `get_column_policy`, `get_health_score`, `get_incident`,
93	  `get_near_misses`, `get_notification_config`, `get_pipeline_status`, `get_run_results`,
94	  `get_run_status`, `get_suite_performance`, `get_suite_results`, `list_assets`,
95	  `list_check_versions`, `list_checks`, `list_connections`, `list_incidents`, `list_runs`,
96	  `list_schedules`, `list_suites`, `list_trigger_bindings`.
97	- **18 that change state** — `create_check`, `update_check`, `delete_check`, `snooze_check`,
98	  `restore_check_version`, `trigger_suite_run`, `cancel_run`, `update_suite`, `set_column_policy`,
99	  `create_schedule`, `update_schedule`, `delete_schedule`, `create_trigger_binding`,
100	  `update_trigger_binding`, `delete_trigger_binding`, `ack_incident`, `resolve_incident`,
101	  `import_suite`. All gate on `edit` access to the affected suite (the schedule, binding and
102	  incident tools via the suite they target); `import_suite` additionally requires the **member**
103	  workspace role, since it has no existing suite to gate on.
104	- **5 that persist nothing but open a live datasource connection using stored credentials** —
105	  `profile_column`, `list_columns`, `dryrun_check`, `suggest_column_policy`, `test_connection`.
106	  These are gated like writes, not like reads, because they spend a real credential against a
107	  remote system even though nothing is saved: the first four require `edit` on the suite whose
108	  connection they probe, and `test_connection` (which has no suite at all) requires the **member**
109	  workspace role.
110	
111	`get_adf_pipeline_status` predates dbt (ADR 0029) and Airflow support and was never ADF-only
112	despite the name; `get_pipeline_status` is the current name and states its actual scope. The old
113	name stays registered — a client with it pinned in a saved prompt or static config keeps
114	working — and delegates to `get_pipeline_status` with identical behavior. New integrations
115	should use `get_pipeline_status` ([#1443](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/1443)).
116	
117	No MCP tool is Admin-only. Every Admin-only capability in ADR 0033's authorization matrix is a
118	connection *mutation* (create/edit/delete/re-auth), and none of those are exposed here at all —
119	a credential must never transit an LLM. `test_connection` reports only whether a live probe
120	succeeded; it never returns a credential or a secret reference (Tier 1 + Tier 2 expansion, issue
121	[#529](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/529)).
122	
123	### Reading the results honestly
124	
125	A REST caller wrote their own query and a UI user reads the screen — the row
126	count, the timestamps, the "running" badge, the filter they chose. An AI client
127	has neither, so several tools return **fields whose whole job is to say what the
128	answer does not cover**. A well-behaved client should branch on these rather
129	than summarising the payload as-is.
130	
131	| Field | Appears on | What it prevents |
132	|---|---|---|
133	| `total` · `returned` · `truncated` | `list_runs`, `list_checks`, `list_check_versions`, `list_incidents`, `list_assets`, `get_check_history`, `get_pipeline_status` | reporting one page as the whole set. `truncated` is computed against a real total, never inferred from page length. The unpaged tools — `list_suites`, `list_connections`, `list_schedules`, `list_trigger_bindings`, `get_near_misses` — return every row and carry no page fields at all |

### Part A — silent honesty gaps
None found. The core change is clean:

- **Alias correctness verified mechanically, not just by inspection.** `@mcp.tool` in this FastMCP version is an identity decorator (`type(foo) is function`, confirmed by running it), so `get_adf_pipeline_status`'s body calling `get_pipeline_status(...)` is a genuine plain-Python delegate — no double-dispatch, no divergent validation, no divergent error path. The new test `test_get_adf_pipeline_status_is_a_working_alias_for_get_pipeline_status` (`backend/tests/mcp/test_mcp_tools.py`) asserts full-payload equality between the two calls, which is the right proof for "identical behavior" rather than just checking the docstring says so.
- **The alias's docstring claim is true**: "same arguments, same return shape" — signatures are byte-identical (`provider`, `status`, `limit: Annotated[int, Field(ge=1,le=200)]=20`, `offset: Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)]=0`), and since the alias body is a pure passthrough, validation errors (`ToolError` on bad `provider`/`status`) surface identically.
- **Tool-selection honesty (Part B, but confirmed against real code)**: the alias's opening sentence — *"Deprecated alias for `get_pipeline_status` — use that tool instead."* — is exactly the disambiguation-in-first-sentence pattern the review asks for; a client seeing only the first line still won't pick it by default.
- **`mcp_gates.GATES`** correctly declares both names as `"read"`, and `test_every_mcp_tool_declares_a_gate_and_the_registry_matches` (`backend/tests/api/test_role_enforcement.py:433`) enforces `tools == set(GATES)`, so the alias can't silently escape the gate sweep — confirmed this test exists and would fail if either name were missing.

### Part A — stale neighbour docstrings
None found inside `backend/app/mcp/server.py`. Grepped the whole file for any other tool's docstring naming `get_adf_pipeline_status` (e.g. a "see X" cross-reference from `create_trigger_binding`/`list_trigger_bindings`/`get_near_misses`) — there are none, so no sibling docstring is falsified by the rename.

None — the alias forwards all four parameters unmodified, all four are read by `get_pipeline_status`.

None introduced; no new field, no new `Decimal`/`datetime`.

`docs/site/mcp-setup.md` is internally consistent: 24+18+5=47 sums correctly, the read-only bullet list, the two honesty-fields tables (`total`/`truncated`/`oldest_in_page`), and the "workflow question → tool" table all use `get_pipeline_status` as the canonical name and correctly *omit* the deprecated alias from the question-routing table (appropriate — you don't want to steer new callers toward a deprecated tool). `docs/site/changelog.md` and `docs/progress.md` line up with the rename and with each other.

Purely cosmetic, doesn't affect any sweep (all four sweeps iterate the dict via `tools_with_gate`, which sorts), but worth a one-line fixup since the file's own comment documents the convention.

The four files under review were updated correctly (46→47), but a repo-wide grep for `"46 tools"`/`"46 curated"` turns up **eight more places still saying 46** that this exact project has a documented habit of updating alongside every prior tool-count change (ADR 0008's own amendment log, `README.md` ×2, `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/site/feature-matrix.md`, `docs/site/glossary.md`, `docs/site/deployment-parity.md`, `docs/site/adr/README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` ×2).
